web_title: 2. What Bloom Energy Does: Product, Revenue Categories & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: “I am delighted that there is strong market recognition that the Bloom Energy platform is the ideal choice for powering AI data centers.” [19]
epigraph.author: K.R. Sridhar, Founder, Chairman and CEO

web_blocks.text: Start with the reporting boundary. Bloom’s SEC filings describe one operating and reportable segment; they do not disclose separate segments for fuel cells, data centers, electrolyzers, utilities or international markets. The consolidated business is disaggregated by revenue category—product, installation, service and electricity. These are not stand-alone segments: they are the company’s revenue disaggregation categories, principally under ASC 606, and identify different accounting promises and delivery patterns inside one customer solution. The sole reportable segment therefore represents 100% of consolidated revenue; Bloom does not disclose a separate segment-profit allocation or segment-profit measure, so consolidated operating profit must not be presented as an independently allocated segment result. Electricity revenue also includes some lease arrangements outside ASC 606. [1][2] The only fact supplied by the permitted sanitized fundamentals card is the sector label Industrials; all operating measures below come from cited primary filings and company releases. [1][2]

The core product is the Energy Server, a stationary solid-oxide fuel-cell system. At the cell, fuel and oxygen participate in an electrochemical reaction that generates direct-current electricity and heat without combustion in the cell. A commercial system adds fuel handling or processing, stacks, modules, controls, power conditioning and connections to the customer’s electrical system. Bloom says its platform can use natural gas, biogas or hydrogen, subject to system configuration and the availability and specification of fuel. It is therefore an onsite generator, not a battery and not zero-input energy. If the site uses natural gas, fuel-related emissions remain part of the system’s lifecycle profile. [1][7][11][12]

The system’s operating proposition is firm onsite output close to the load. A data center, semiconductor fab or hospital may place high value on continuity, power quality or the ability to build before a conventional grid connection is ready. Bloom’s marketing emphasizes modular scaling and onsite resilience; the FY2025 10-K cautions that actual customer economics depend on local gas supply, alternative electricity cost, tariffs, permits, financing and performance. A good analysis separates those two statements: the product is designed to address a real reliability and time-to-power need, while whether it is the best solution depends on site-specific comparisons. [1][24][25]

Product revenue is primarily equipment revenue. Bloom sells Energy Servers to end users, project financiers and strategic or channel partners; the end user who consumes electricity may not be the party to whom Bloom invoices equipment. The revenue line also includes sales under different purchase and financing options, each with its own contractual responsibilities. In FY2025, product revenue was $1,531.281 million, up 41.1% from $1,085.153 million in FY2024. The company attributed the increase mainly to demand driven by customers’ time-to-power needs, with some effect from share-based consideration promised in connection with a hyperscaler customer. [1]

Installation revenue is project revenue tied to installing systems at customer sites when Bloom undertakes that work. Installation can require civil and electrical work, local contractors, interconnection, permits and customer coordination. The line can vary materially with the size and timing of projects and which party performs the work. FY2025 installation revenue was $204.068 million, up 66.8% from $122.318 million in FY2024. In Q3 2026, installation gross margin was negative 4.8%, illustrating that the activity is not automatically profitable simply because the equipment sale is attractive. [1][3]

Service revenue represents operations-and-maintenance agreements and related obligations. The company monitors systems and provides maintenance and, under some contracts, output- or efficiency-related performance warranties and guarantees. Service revenue is recognized over the service period. Bloom’s FY2025 filing says O&M arrangements range from five to twenty years, while extension options may be renewed or canceled annually; it also says nearly every customer historically renewed. In FY2025 service revenue was $228.295 million, compared with $213.542 million in FY2024. In the first nine months of 2026, service revenue reached $198.459 million, with the filing attributing growth partly to a larger installed base and higher performance-guarantee costs. [1][2]

Electricity revenue arises in arrangements where Bloom retains or participates in revenue from electricity generated by Energy Server assets, including certain lease arrangements and legacy managed-service or PPA structures. The line is smaller than equipment sales and can reflect asset ownership and one-time project changes rather than a pure recurring usage trend. FY2025 electricity revenue was $60.350 million compared with $52.843 million in 2024; the 10-K says the increase was mainly due to a one-time customer-contract settlement after asset redeployment, partly offset by lower straight-line revenue associated with repowering certain sites. That detail matters because a revenue increase in this category need not indicate higher recurring electricity output. [1]

web_blocks.caption: Revenue disaggregation categories (one reportable segment; USD millions; electricity includes lease revenue) [1][2]
web_blocks.takeaway: Product was the largest reported category in both the annual and nine-month periods. The table does not imply separate operating segments; each line reflects a revenue-recognition category within the consolidated business.

web_blocks.text: The nine-month comparison reveals how rapidly mix can shift. Product revenue rose from $892.794 million in the first nine months of 2025 to $2,662.371 million in the first nine months of 2026, while total revenue increased from $1,246.311 million to $3,052.256 million. Electricity revenue declined over that comparison, in part for specific project and asset-related reasons described in the 10-Q. The snapshot is a period comparison, not a normalized run-rate: it spans a sharp growth period, project milestones and changes in the financing and ownership profile. [2]

Bloom’s customer examples help place the product within distinct use cases. At Unimicron’s Taoyuan semiconductor facility, Bloom’s case page describes a 600-kW Energy Server installation operating in parallel with the utility, with first installation completed in August 2023 and later expansion contemplated. This illustrates a critical manufacturing load in which clean-room processes, chillers and voltage quality can matter; the vendor page’s account is not a third-party return-on-investment audit. [17]

Equinix demonstrates a larger and longer data-center relationship. Bloom reported that a 1-MW pilot at one Silicon Valley site in 2015 was followed by deployments at 19 U.S. International Business Exchange data centers in six states. In February 2025, Bloom said the arrangement exceeded 100 MW, with approximately 75 MW operational and 30 MW under construction. The status breakdown is more informative than the headline alone because it distinguishes electricity-producing installations from projects awaiting completion. [18]

Utility- and hyperscaler-linked channels show another form of demand. AEP placed an initial 100-MW order inside a supply agreement for up to 1 GW in 2024. Oracle’s 2026 release described an initial 1.2 GW as contracted and deploying within a broader master services agreement for up to 2.8 GW. NTT DATA announced 900 MW with initial shipments expected in 2027. Each release uses different commitment language. You should not sum frameworks and future deployments into current sales, nor assume that all sales are made directly to the final electricity user. [19][20][21]

Electrolysis is a related application, not the reverse side of the same revenue line. A fuel cell consumes fuel to generate electricity; an electrolyzer consumes electricity and water to make hydrogen. Bloom’s product page says its solid-oxide system can incorporate high-temperature heat and reports laboratory or product-comparison performance claims. The Department of Energy’s multi-year plan identifies hydrogen production and fuel-cell technology as separate research and development areas. For Bloom, the engineering relationship may offer common manufacturing knowledge, yet commercial proof still requires projects with available input energy, compliant design, hydrogen distribution or offtake, and repeatable service. [8][9][14]

Management’s AI-power narrative is explicit: Sridhar called the platform “the ideal choice for powering AI data centers” in the AEP announcement. That quote explains management’s target customer, not the whole business. Bloom continues to report one segment and serves multiple commercial and industrial verticals. A rigorous description therefore keeps the product definition stable, reports revenue categories as categories, names verified installations, and distinguishes actual operating MW from announced or contracted programs. [1][19]

For a customer, the buying unit is not necessarily one stack or one module. The practical system is sized to a site’s demand and installed in modular increments, then integrated with existing utility service or designed for an islanded microgrid. Bloom’s technology page explains the building-block sequence from fuel cell to stack to module to Energy Server platform. This design can help the buyer stage capacity, but the scale-up still depends on site footprint, gas infrastructure, electrical switchgear, permits and construction sequencing. “Modular” describes product architecture; it does not mean that every site can add a module without engineering or approvals. [7][24][25]

Customer contracts also distribute responsibilities differently. A direct system sale places equipment ownership with the customer; a traditional lease may place ownership with a financing partner; a PPA or managed-service arrangement can link payments to power or capacity while Bloom provides operations and maintenance. The FY2025 filing explains that contract combination and revenue recognition depend on which parties buy equipment and extended service. Thus one deployment may produce a large initial product transaction and years of recognized service, while another may leave Bloom recognizing some electricity revenue. Comparing customer announcements requires attention to the contractual counterparty and asset owner. [1]

There is a further accounting nuance in hyperscaler arrangements. Bloom’s Q3 2026 filing describes share-based consideration payable to a customer’s customer in connection with the Oracle relationship and says the associated amount is recognized as a reduction of revenue as related Energy Server systems are delivered. This is a contract-level acquisition cost recorded through revenue, not a conventional manufacturing cost per unit. You should include it when evaluating the economic terms of customer acquisition, even though it does not change the company’s four-category segment reporting. [2]

A customer voice clarifies what is being purchased. In the AEP announcement, Sridhar said the platform was “the ideal choice for powering AI data centers.” That is a management statement and should be treated as a strategy claim. By contrast, Equinix’s vice president of energy operations said the fuel cells allowed the company to generate “cleaner and reliable electricity onsite” at data centers. The second quote supplies customer rationale but still does not disclose a complete system-level cost comparison. Use executive quotations to understand the buying problem; rely on filings and completed-project evidence to test the financial and operational outcome. [18][19]

The concrete cases vary in both scale and proof. Unimicron is a 600-kW semiconductor-facility installation described in a Bloom case study; Equinix reports a 2015 pilot expanded to multiple U.S. data centers; AEP placed an initial 100-MW order under an up-to-1-GW arrangement; Oracle separated its first 1.2-GW tranche from a 2.8-GW maximum; and NTT DATA’s first shipments were expected in 2027. You should keep those examples in chronological order and preserve each status qualifier. A named logo or capacity headline is not equivalent to a fully operating site. [17][18][19][20][21]

Bloom’s opportunity is tied to loads for which time, reliability and power quality matter, but the customer portfolio is wider than hyperscale computing. The company and its filings describe semiconductor manufacturing, healthcare, retail, campuses, utilities and other commercial and industrial uses. A semiconductor facility values process continuity; a hospital may prioritize critical-load resilience; a data center may need a large block of power before a grid upgrade is complete. You should not assume identical buying criteria across verticals. Each vertical has different load profiles, permitting conditions, fuel economics and downtime costs, which can affect both deployment design and willingness to finance the equipment. [1][17][24][25]

DOE’s basic fuel-cell description helps you separate the physical process from Bloom’s particular implementation. Fuel cells use an electrochemical reaction; the fuel and electrolyte determine operating temperature, fuel tolerance and application. DOE’s fuel-cell-system material also points to fuel processors and electrical power conditioners, which consume space, add cost and influence overall system efficiency. This is why comparisons should use whole-system performance and maintenance rather than a cell-only efficiency figure. Bloom’s claims about high efficiency and fuel flexibility are relevant, but they need to be tested at the operating system boundary and under a customer’s actual fuel and load conditions. [10][11][12][13]

An electrolyzer project is a different revenue and customer problem from an Energy Server deployment. The customer supplies electricity and water to produce hydrogen; then the hydrogen must be stored, transported or used by an industrial offtaker. Bloom’s launch release cited efficiency advantages, but those are company claims and the cost of electricity is central to the end product. DOE’s hydrogen program plan separately addresses production and infrastructure priorities. You should therefore assess electrolyzer commercialization through installed capacity, utilization, input-energy contracts and hydrogen offtake rather than assuming that fuel-cell deployments automatically create electrolyzer sales. [8][9][14]

The evidence hierarchy in this chapter is deliberate. SEC filings establish one reportable segment and the recognized revenue categories. Company releases and customer case studies establish what the parties say about selected deployments. DOE and EIA resources describe fuel-cell technology and the broader electricity system. When these sources differ in purpose, keep the claim within its source’s boundary. In particular, vendor-reported efficiency, uptime, carbon and “time-to-power” benefits should be labeled as claims until independently measured for the specific installation. [1][2][10][15][17][18]

An end-to-end example is Unimicron’s Taoyuan semiconductor facility. Bloom’s case study says the customer sought onsite power for production needs exposed to outages, voltage drops and uninterrupted clean-room and chiller operations. The installed product is a 600-kW Bloom Energy Server, connected in parallel with the utility; Bloom says it delivered the system five months after order and commissioned it three weeks later, in August 2023. The case study says the customer contemplated further expansion through 2027, but that is not treated as installed capacity. The document does not disclose unit price, ownership, financing, tariff, service fee or payment terms, so none is inferred; it also does not identify a specific Energy Server generation. [17]

book_paragraphs: You can understand the Energy Server as a complete stationary power system rather than a stack in a box. The cell converts chemical energy through an electrochemical reaction; modules group cells into a deployable unit; the system adds fuel management, controls and power conditioning; and the site requires electrical integration and commissioning. DOE’s description of fuel-cell systems is useful here because it makes the support equipment visible. If you compare technologies only at cell level, you will miss part of the cost, efficiency and reliability question that the customer actually buys. [7][11][12]

Keep the customer problem in view. A facility may want continuous onsite generation because grid capacity is late, power quality is critical or backup arrangements are burdensome. Bloom’s site describes data centers and other high-load customers, while its filings also refer to manufacturing, utilities and commercial facilities. You should ask what problem each buyer is solving. A semiconductor plant, hospital and data center do not have identical load shapes, downtime tolerances, gas availability or regulatory requirements. One product family may address several applications, but the implementation and economics can differ sharply by site. [1][24][25]

The product category is the largest source of recognized sales. Bloom reported $1,531.281 million of product revenue in FY2025, compared with $1,085.153 million in FY2024. The nine-month 2026 comparison was $2,662.371 million versus $892.794 million in the first nine months of 2025. When you see those figures, remember what they represent: products transferred under contracts, not the full lifetime power produced by every system. The product line can be lumpy because a large site may cross a delivery milestone in one period and another tranche in a later period. [1][2]

Installation is a separate category because delivering a system to a site and making it operate are not the same promise. The project may require engineering, construction, gas connection, interconnection, commissioning and customer acceptance. FY2025 installation revenue was $204.068 million, up from $122.318 million in 2024, while Q3 2026 installation gross margin was negative 4.8%. That margin is one quarter, not a universal result. Still, it demonstrates the need to study field execution independently from product manufacturing. You should look for installation margin by cohort and whether factory standardization reduces rework, labor and delays. [1][3]

Service is what happens after the system is in the field. Bloom’s filings describe monitoring, operations and maintenance, warranty support and performance commitments. FY2025 service revenue was $228.295 million; the first nine months of 2026 produced $198.459 million. Optional annual maintenance renewals have historically been high, according to Bloom, but contracts can include annual termination rights and guarantees can reduce revenue or increase cost when promised output is missed. You should view the growing service line as an installed-base opportunity and an ongoing technical test at the same time. A bigger fleet means more future service revenue only if it remains maintainable at a reasonable cost. [1][2]

Electricity revenue is smaller and more sensitive to ownership structure. It reached $60.350 million in 2025, but the 10-K explains that the annual increase included a one-time settlement after assets were redeployed. That should stop you from interpreting it as a simple recurring-use curve. In some structures Bloom sells equipment and service, in others financing partners hold the systems, and in some legacy arrangements Bloom recognizes electricity or lease-related revenue. The accounting line tells you what the contract produced for Bloom, not necessarily the amount paid by the final end user for all electricity. [1]

Use the revenue table as a map, not as a set of businesses. Bloom reports a single segment. The table reconciles the four categories to total company revenue in 2024, 2025 and the first nine months of 2025 and 2026. You can see product become a much larger share in 2026, while service grows with the base and electricity falls in that nine-month comparison. To explain those movements, follow product shipments, project settlements, asset ownership and billing. Without that contract context, you could mistake changes in revenue recognition for a shift in the underlying customer demand. [1][2]

Equinix gives you a rarer longitudinal example. The relationship began with 1 MW at one data center in 2015, according to Bloom, and exceeded 100 MW across 19 sites by 2025. Bloom reported 75 MW operational and 30 MW under construction. This combination of a customer quote, a time series and installed status is stronger evidence than a single megawatt announcement. Yet you still need to distinguish the customer’s testimony about cleaner and reliable onsite power from an independent lifecycle assessment or disclosed customer payback calculation. [18]

AEP, Oracle and NTT DATA illustrate how project counterparties differ. AEP’s agreement began with a 100-MW order under a framework of up to 1 GW. Oracle described 1.2 GW contracted and deploying, inside a 2.8-GW master agreement. NTT DATA announced 900 MW across future data-center projects, with initial shipments expected in 2027. You should not roll these into one installed-base number. One is an initial order, another has a defined contracted tranche plus a maximum framework, and the third points to future shipments. Maintaining these distinctions is essential to a price-blind but evidence-based operating assessment. [19][20][21]

Contract architecture also explains revenue adjustments. The 2026 10-Q says Bloom committed share-based consideration to a customer’s customer in connection with Oracle and recognizes the associated consideration as a reduction of revenue as related systems are delivered. You should view that as part of customer acquisition economics, rather than trying to read product gross margin in isolation. The arrangement is still within the same reported segment and categories; it does not create a separate AI business line in the accounting. [2]

Finally, keep fuel-cell generation separate from hydrogen electrolysis. In the first, fuel flows in and electricity is produced. In the second, electricity and water are inputs and hydrogen is the product. Bloom promotes its high-temperature electrolyzer as an extension of the same platform, but the customer needs an affordable electricity supply and a reliable hydrogen offtaker. DOE treats these as connected but distinct areas in its research plan. You should test the electrolyzer business on delivered units, utilization and offtake, not infer success from the installed Energy Server base. [8][9][14]

When a CEO says the platform is ideal for AI data centers, listen for the strategic intent and then ask what evidence would confirm it. The useful evidence is named customers, order status, completed and accepted systems, service performance and diversified sales. Bloom has all four revenue categories, multiple customer verticals and long-term relationships, but it reports one segment and has not published complete per-vertical economics. Your description should preserve that boundary. [1][19]

When you read the product table, note that it contains four rows but one company segment. The FY2025 revenue figures—$1,531.281 million product, $204.068 million installation, $228.295 million service and $60.350 million electricity—sum to $2,023.994 million. The nine-month 2026 figures—$2,662.371 million, $161.764 million, $198.459 million and $29.662 million—sum to $3,052.256 million. These exact amounts let you reconcile the business’s recognized activity without inventing a data-center segment. The sole reportable segment accounts for 100% of consolidated revenue, but Bloom does not disclose a separate segment-profit allocation; consolidated EBIT is not a separately allocated segment-profit measure. [1][2]

The revenue categories also answer different questions. Product revenue tells you the value of systems transferred under contracts. Installation revenue identifies project work and milestone timing. Service revenue reflects work over time for an installed base. Electricity revenue reflects a smaller set of ownership and lease arrangements. You should never add service backlog to product backlog or assume that every customer’s electricity payments are booked by Bloom as electricity revenue; the contractual counterparty and accounting treatment matter. The 10-K describes maintenance renewal options, financing alternatives and lease arrangements as separate features of the contract architecture. [1]

Now compare the customer stories by what they prove. Unimicron’s 600-kW site documents a specified manufacturing installation and commissioning date, but it is a case study written by Bloom. Equinix’s 1-MW pilot-to-more-than-100-MW timeline provides a longer repeat-deployment example and separates 75 MW operating from 30 MW under construction. AEP’s 100-MW first order, Oracle’s 1.2-GW contracted tranche and NTT DATA’s future 900-MW program demonstrate broader commercial interest at different status levels. You should use the cases to form hypotheses about buyer needs, then use audited revenue and actual installation status to test conversion. [17][18][19][20][21]

The buyer’s direct quotation is useful but bounded. Sridhar called the Energy Server “the ideal choice for powering AI data centers.” You should translate that sentence into observable questions: Does the system meet the data center’s load? Was it permitted? Did equipment arrive and commission on schedule? Does the customer expand at additional sites? What do service expense and customer acceptance look like? The quote expresses management’s conviction, whereas the operating record must establish whether the product’s reliability and deployment speed continue to win and retain customers. [19]

Finally, keep the product family’s adjacencies in their proper place. A fuel cell converts fuel to electricity, while an electrolyzer consumes electricity to produce hydrogen. A shared solid-oxide platform can support engineering synergies, yet the hydrogen sale requires available electricity, water, a customer able to use hydrogen and a delivery or storage pathway. You should evaluate each business loop separately even if manufacturing and research overlap. This distinction prevents an announcement about hydrogen technology from being mistaken for evidence that a large, recurring hydrogen segment is already operating. [1][8][9][14]

You should also distinguish an installed customer from a customer that has simply signed a framework. The annual report explains that Bloom recognizes product revenue when the relevant transfer-of-control conditions are met, while installation, service and electricity may have separate or combined contract treatment depending on parties and obligations. That means customer counts, backlog, recognized revenue and installed megawatts are different lenses. When you build a business model later, keep them separate and link each to a date and source; do not infer a recurring annual sale from a single customer announcement. [1][2]

Use Unimicron as your end-to-end customer example, but keep the limits visible. Bloom describes a semiconductor manufacturer facing outages and voltage drops that could disrupt clean-room processes and chillers. The case page identifies a 600-kW Energy Server at Taoyuan, operating in parallel with the utility; Bloom says delivery followed the order by five months and commissioning took three weeks, with operation beginning in August 2023. You do not know the unit price, financing terms, tariff, service charge or payment schedule: the case study does not disclose them. It also does not identify a specific Energy Server generation. You should not fill those gaps with industry averages or inferred savings. [17]

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: You now have a more accurate answer to “what does Bloom sell?” It sells a power system and the services, installation work and financing structures that make the system usable at a customer’s site. The four revenue categories explain accounting, not four independently measured businesses. When you hear a large customer megawatt number, pause and ask whether it is installed, under construction, contracted or merely within a framework. That discipline protects you from mistaking a compelling customer story for audited segment disclosure.
